From Middle English ese, eise, aise, from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (“elbow room; opportunity”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais, Italian agio and asio, Sicilian aciu and Portuguese azo.

senses.d: Lack of difficulty; the ability to do something easily.
ex: He played the ukelele with ease.
The ease of lifting the weight, despite lack of skill, came from her pure strength.

senses.d: Freedom from pain, hardship, and annoyance, sometimes (derogatory, archaic) idleness, sloth.
ex: She enjoyed the ease of living in a house where the servants did all the work.

senses.d: Freedom from worry and concern; peace; sometimes (derogatory, archaic) indifference.
ex: The pension set her mind at ease.

senses.d: Freedom from effort; leisure, rest.
ex: We took our ease on the patio.

senses.d: Freedom from financial effort or worry; affluence.
ex: His inheritance catapulted him into a life of ease.

senses.d: Freedom from embarrassment or awkwardness; grace.
ex: She dealt with the faculty with combined authority and ease.

senses.d: Followed by of or from: release from or reduction of pain, hardship, or annoyance.
ex: Take one pill every 12 hours to provide ease from pain.

senses.d: Release from intestinal discomfort: defecation.
Release from constraint, obligation, or a constrained position.
ex: At ease, soldier!

senses.d: Additional space provided to allow greater movement.
ex: Add some ease to the waist measurement.

senses.d: To free (something) from pain, worry, agitation, etc.
ex: He eased his conscience by confessing.

senses.d: To alleviate, assuage or lessen (pain).
ex: Sunny / Yesterday my life was filled with rain / Sunny / You smiled at me and really eased the pain

senses.d: To give respite to (someone).
ex: The provision of extra staff eased their workload.

senses.d: To loosen or slacken the tension on a line.
ex: We eased the boom vang, then lowered the sail.

senses.d: To reduce the difficulty of (something).
ex: We had to ease the entry requirements.
I want to thank you all for easing my coming out.

senses.d: To move (something) slowly and carefully.
ex: He eased the cork from the bottle.
Ease down off boulders; a jump may jar or sprain.

senses.d: To lessen in intensity.
ex: The pain eased overnight.

senses.d: To proceed with little effort.
ex: The car eased onto the motorway.

senses.d: To reduce speed.
To take something from (a person), especially by robbery.

senses.d: Comfortable; at ease.
ex: Now that I know it's taken care of, I can rest easy at night.

senses.d: Requiring little skill or effort.
ex: It's often easy to wake up but hard to get up.
The teacher gave an easy test to her students.

senses.d: Causing ease; giving comfort, or freedom from care or labour.
ex: Rich people live in easy circumstances, that is, the easy life.
an easy chair

senses.d: Free from constraint, harshness, or formality; unconstrained; smooth.
ex: easy manners; an easy style
the easy vigour of a line

senses.d: Consenting readily to sex.
ex: She has a reputation for being easy; they say she slept with half the senior class.

senses.d: Not making resistance or showing unwillingness; tractable; yielding; compliant.
ex: He gain'd their easy hearts.
He is[…] too tyrannical to be an easy monarch.

senses.d: Not straitened as to money matters; opposed to tight.
ex: The market is easy.

senses.d: In a relaxed or casual manner.
ex: After his illness, John decided to take it easy.
Everything comes easy to her.

senses.d: In a manner without strictness or harshness; gently; softly.
ex: Jane went easier on him after he broke his arm.

senses.d: Handily; at the very least.
ex: This project will cost 15 million dollars, easy.

senses.d: Something that is easy.
ex: Virtually all of the "easies" are the first watermark and the "toughs" are the second.
